opening.headline: When reducing service scale to zero in an attempt to lower idle costs, we explore methods for evaluating cold start issues from the perspectives of boot time and request paths.
body: Even though traffic is nearly nonexistent during nighttime, pods and GPUs remain running, leading to high costs. Setting the value to zero eliminates costs, but the next request must start from scratch, resulting in the full startup time being reflected as user delay.

In this lesson, we will examine route optimization to reduce request path overhead, the principle of scale-to-zero to minimize replica count to zero, and resource and probe configurations that affect startup time. Finally, we will work through a case study on whether to reduce overnight idle service usage to zero.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the principles of route optimization and scale-to-zero.
Can assess the cost benefits and risk of downtime associated with scale-to-zero.

screens.title: We want to reduce idle costs, but cold start is a concern.
screens.lead: Examine the traffic patterns for day and night, as well as the initial request's journey through the routing segments, in the diagram. Look for the point where cost and delay move in opposite directions.

visual.alt: A graph overlaying traffic volume by time period with pod count, indicating overnight idle periods and the latency delay of the first request.
labels: Cost when Pard is maintained continuously
Deployment time: scheduling + model loading + probe passage

paragraphs: Internal services are heavily used during the day but see almost no requests at night. Yet, pods and GPUs remain running throughout the day, incurring costs equivalent to overnight idle periods.

Reducing the replication count to zero lowers this cost. However, when the next request arrives, the service must start from scratch. This startup time is directly reflected as user delay. The overhead from the endpoint front path also contributes to the delay.
The desire to reduce costs meets concern about cold starts. The question of this lesson is how to evaluate this trade-off.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: If users who send their first request in the evening have to wait several minutes, should the service response time be reduced to zero? The decision criterion depends on the nature of the service.

screens.outro: First, let's consider whether our own service can be reduced to zero.

screens.title: Can the service be reduced to zero during periods of no traffic?
screens.lead: When you select a question, the instructor's thought process unfolds. Please don't submit or input anything yet—first reflect on your own service, then try it.

items.prompt: How long does it take for our service to respond to the first request?
items.answer: This includes not only the time when the pod comes up, but also scheduling, image and model loading, and probe passage. For large models, model loading typically accounts for the majority of the time. Without knowing the exact numbers, there is still no basis for assuming a zero value.

items.prompt: What do users see during that time?
items.answer: The request may be terminated due to a timeout or may remain stalled on the screen for an extended period. It is necessary to verify whether the system displays a waiting time indicator and whether the calling side's timeout duration is longer than the system's operational timeout.

items.prompt: Is a service acceptable if capacity is not guaranteed?
items.answer: Reducing services down to zero may result in insufficient capacity when they are scaled back up. The decision depends on whether the service is one that must always respond in operations or an internal non-critical service.

screens.outro: Let's first look at route optimization, a method for reducing delay in the requested path.

screens.title: route optimization: reducing delay in requested paths
screens.lead: Select each tab to learn what route optimization is and the conditions and constraints associated with it.

visual.alt: Diagram comparing the general path and the optimized path.

tabs.label: something
tabs.body: When route optimization is enabled, Databricks Model Serving improves the network path for inference requests, enabling the client and model to communicate more directly. The goal is to achieve higher QPS than with standard endpoints, with greater stability and lower latency. The reduction refers to overhead latency before requests reach the model, not to model computation time.

tabs.label: Calling convention
tabs.body: The optimized endpoint calls differently from a standard endpoint. It uses a different URL and authenticates with a Databricks OAuth token. Personal access tokens are not supported. Therefore, before enabling it, you must verify whether the authentication method and address configuration on the calling side can be changed.

tabs.label: Turning on moment
tabs.body: This feature can only be enabled when creating an endpoint. Existing endpoints cannot be converted into optimized endpoints. To enable route optimization, select the route optimization option in the creation screen or specify `route_optimized: true` in the creation request. To apply this to an existing service, a new endpoint must be created and migrated.

tabs.label: Scope of application
tabs.body: This is available only for custom model serving endpoints and feature serving endpoints. Endpoints using Foundation Model APIs or external models are not supported. Route optimization reduces latency in the request path, so please note that it does not directly address cold start issues.

screens.outro: Now let's follow the structure of scale-to-zero and cold start by reducing the replica count to zero.

screens.title: The principle of scale-to-zero and the flow wherein deployment time is reflected in latency
screens.lead: Let's walk through the process step by step from no request to the first request arriving and responding. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

visual.alt: Timeline showing the time flow from zero replicas to the first request arriving, the pod coming online, and responding.

steps.title: Method of reduction to zero
steps.body: Scale-to-zero is a method that reduces the replica count to zero when the service is not in use. The serving endpoint is enabled using settings such as `scale_to_zero_enabled`. The advantage is that there are no costs incurred while the service is not being used.

steps.title: In 0, capacity is not guaranteed.
steps.body: When scaled down to zero, capacity is not guaranteed and additional delays occur when the resource scales back up, resulting in a cold start. For this reason, the documentation advises against using scale-to-zero on operational endpoints.

steps.title: Zero-scale expansion in Kubernetes
steps.body: To set `minReplicas` to 0 in Kubernetes HPA, the `HPAScaleToZero` feature gate is required and must be used in conjunction with custom metrics or external metrics. As previously mentioned, KEDA supports zero scaling by default because its default value for `minReplicaCount` is 0.

steps.title: Composition of Cold Start Time
steps.body: When the first request arrives, scheduling, image and model loading, and initial probe completion occur sequentially. The cold start time is the sum of these three phases. It includes not only the time it takes for the container to start, but also the actual time it takes for the application to be ready.

steps.title: The probe determines traffic reception.
steps.body: After the startup probe succeeds, the readiness probe and active probe are initiated. The pod only begins receiving traffic after the readiness probe passes. Therefore, requests do not reach this pod until model loading is complete, resulting in user wait time.

steps.title: Exposed due to user delay
steps.body: Ultimately, the delay of the first request is the value obtained by adding the route overhead to the cold start time. Route optimization reduces the number of subsequent steps, while the initial steps are determined by image size, model loading, and probe configuration.

screens.outro: We will check term by term the resources and probe settings that affect the dwell time.

screens.title: Resources and probe settings that affect dwell time
screens.lead: Hover over or select an underlined term in the description below to see a short description. Check the terms one by one.

data.text: The pod specs requests serves as the scheduling baseline, while limits represents the resource usage ceiling. When limits is exceeded, the CPU is throttled and memory results in an OOM (Out of Memory) termination. If all containers have identical CPU and memory limits of requests and limits, they are assigned the Guaranteed priority; otherwise, they are assigned Burstable or BestEffort priority and are evicted from the node when resource shortages occur starting from BestEffort. When upgrading a model server to a new version, the deployment replaces pods at a controlled pace by increasing the new ReplicaSet and decreasing the old ReplicaSet. During this process, Start probe waits for slow initialization, Preparation probe allows traffic only after being ready, and Active probe restarts containers that become stuck. Misconfigured Active probe can trigger restarts under heavy load, potentially leading to cascading failures.

terms.tip: This is the criterion used by the scheduler to determine which node to place a pod on. If the model server's requests are high, it may take longer to find an appropriate node, or additional nodes might need to be provisioned.
This is a limit on usage. When CPU reaches its limit, it is throttled and performance degrades; when memory exceeds its limit, the container is terminated due to OOM (Out of Memory).
This is the QoS class when all containers have the same CPU and memory requests and limits. Containers of this class are evicted last when node resources are insufficient.
This is a QoS level with neither requests nor limits. If node resources are insufficient, it is the first to be evicted.
During deployment, it increases a new ReplicaSet when deploying a new version, reduces the old ReplicaSet, and replaces pods at a controlled pace.
Check if the app has started. If configured, do not proceed with activation and readiness probes until success, thus waiting for a slow initialization similar to model loading.
Check if the pod is ready to receive requests. Traffic will not reach this pod before it passes.
Check if the container is stuck, and if so, restart it. If the restart is too aggressive, it may restart healthy pods as well, leading to a cascading failure.

screens.title: Explanation: Judgment on 0 expansion for nighttime idle service
screens.lead: The course breaks down the process of determining whether to reduce the internal document summarization service to zero. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

visual.alt: A decision flow diagram selecting either 0 scaling or maintaining at least 1 instance, based on the service's delay sensitivity.
labels: Can the first request wait for the dwell time?
At least 1 instance maintained + scale out during off-peak hours
Is it allowed to have no capacity guarantees?

steps.title: situation
steps.body: There is an internal document summarization service. During the day, employees use it, but there are almost no requests at night. Opinions have emerged that the GPU-powered pod remains running overnight, resulting in unnecessary costs, and a decision must be made regarding whether to implement scaling to zero.

steps.title: Step 1: Estimate cost benefits
steps.body: During off-peak hours, GPU pods can also be shut down. You can roughly estimate how many hours in a day have no requests and how much cost pods would consume during those times. This number represents the upper limit of the savings achievable through zero scaling.

steps.title: Step 2: Break down the mobilization time
steps.body:
We break down the startup time into scheduling, image and model loading, and passing the start probe, checking how long each takes. For example, suppose model loading is the dominant factor and takes several minutes. This value is illustrative and must be measured in actual service environments. If the start probe is configured too briefly and fails before loading is complete, the container will restart repeatedly, resulting in longer startup times.

```
startupProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /health
    port: 8000
  periodSeconds: 10
  failureThreshold: 60
```

In this example, the start probe waits up to `periodSeconds × failureThreshold`, i.e., up to 600 seconds, for loading to complete.

steps.title: Step 3: Evaluate the risk
steps.body: A user sending the first request during nighttime investigates whether they are allowed to wait for that duration, or whether capacity guarantees are not required. If the caller's timeout is shorter than the grace period, the first request will inevitably fail. If capacity is unavailable at the moment a request arrives, the grace period might be extended accordingly.

steps.title: Step 4: Decide A, permit it
steps.body: For internal emergency services, zero expansion is allowed. Instead, inform users that their first request may be slow, and set the call-side timeout to be longer than the startup time. This approach allows us to eliminate overnight costs while managing the acceptable level of inconvenience.

steps.title: Step 5: Decide B, maintain it
steps.body: If the service is sensitive to latency, maintain at least one pod and scale out only during off-peak hours. While this incurs only the cost of one additional pod, it eliminates initial request latency. This is a deliberate trade-off prioritizing latency reduction over cost.

steps.title: result
steps.body: 0 Extension involves a trade-off between cost and deployment time, and the nature of the service determines its suitability. The same technology may be appropriate for internal emergency services but inappropriate for customer-facing real-time services.

screens.outro: Lastly, let me summarize the main points.

screens.title: 0 Extension is a trade-off between cost and mobility time.
screens.lead: This lecture consolidates and organizes the request path optimization and the criteria for zero expansion into a single framework.

paragraphs: Route optimization creates a more direct network path between the client and the model, reducing overhead latency and increasing QPS. It can be enabled only when creating endpoints and must be called using other URLs and OAuth tokens. It is available only for custom model serving and feature serving endpoints.

scale-to-zero instead of eliminating idle costs fails to guarantee capacity and introduces cold start delays. The boot time encompasses not just the container startup time, but also scheduling, image and model loading, and probe completion. The start probe must succeed before the active and readiness probes operate, and only after readiness is achieved can traffic be received.

The decision is based on the nature of the service. For non-urgent services that can tolerate delays, the value is set to 0 with a guidance threshold; for services sensitive to delays, at least one unit must be maintained. Regardless of the case, the decision must be based on the actual measured value of the response time.

Going back to the opening scene, the concern between cost and cold start can be transformed from vague worry into measurable numbers. By evaluating two figures—nighttime idle cost and cold start response time—and aligning them with the nature of the service, a decision can be made.

callout.text: 0 Expansion is an exchange of cost for mobility time.

glossary.def: A feature that creates a more direct network path to the endpoint, reducing latency and increasing QPS.
This method reduces the replica count to zero when no requests are received, eliminating idle costs.
This is the additional delay experienced by the first request when rising from 0.
The time until a Pod is ready to accept requests, including scheduling, loading, and passing its probes.
A check that waits for slow initialization and only accepts traffic after being fully prepared.

misconceptions.myth: 0 Extension is a safe setting that only reduces cost.
misconceptions.fact: If reduced to zero, capacity is not guaranteed and cold start delays may occur upon reactivation. Therefore, a warning is provided that this is not recommended for operational endpoints.

misconceptions.myth: Route optimization can be enabled on existing endpoints.
misconceptions.fact: This can only be enabled when creating an endpoint. Existing endpoints cannot be modified, so a new one must be created and moved.

misconceptions.myth: The mobilization time is the start time of the container.
misconceptions.fact: The boot time includes scheduling, image and model loading, and passing the startup probe. For large models, loading often constitutes the largest component.

points: 0 Expansion is an exchange of cost for mobility time.
Route optimization is subject to the constraint that it reduces the overhead of the requested path and can only be enabled at generation time.
0 Expansion results in no guaranteed capacity and causes a cold start.
The runtime consists of scheduling, loading, and probe traversal.
